data.title: Culture and industry clash in Alaska’s seas
data.description:
Centuries of life built around the cycle of the salmon are being disrupted by the trawlers in the frigid northern seas and other factors

The net rose from the heaving Bering Sea swells, packed so tightly with Alaska pollock that their heads squeezed through the webbing.

As the catch spilled onto the deck, other marine life came with it: a skate, crabs, jellyfish and, among the most consequential, salmon — the fish at the center of a growing fight over industrial trawling in Alaska.

“This is a wild capture fishery, so you do run into your nontarget species, and a lot of people have a problem with that,” said Maverick Blake, the boat’s captain. “But this is what it takes to put seafood on the table.”

Blake redirected the boat toward another fishing ground where he hoped to encounter fewer salmon.

Alaska pollock is the second-largest fishery on Earth. It is the fish inside McDonald’s Filet-O-Fish sandwiches and can be turned into fish sticks and imitation crab. The fishery uses methods that it — and McDonald’s — say are aimed at minimizing environmental impacts, but the nets that catch pollock catch other marine life, too.

Bycatch — marine life caught unintentionally while fishers target something else — makes up 2 percent of the pollock fishery’s total catch. At the scale of a fishery that harvests billions of pounds of pollock annually, that can mean hundreds of thousands of salmon. Over the last 10 years, Bering Sea pollock trawlers caught an average of about 18,000 Chinook and 288,000 other salmon a year, almost all of them chum.

Those catches have become especially contentious as salmon runs collapse across western Alaska, where dozens of Alaska Native communities have relied on salmon for generations. The backlash has spread to smaller commercial and charter fishers who say they, too, are bearing the costs of declining stocks. And trawling and bycatch have become prominent issues in Alaska’s midterm elections, with candidates for governor and in the state’s closely watched US Senate contest sparring over how aggressively to restrict the industry.

In 2024, Alaska and Canada instated a seven-year ban on Chinook fishing along the Yukon River — one full salmon life cycle — to give depleted populations a chance to rebuild. The Kuskokwim River has faced repeated Chinook and chum closures too, while other Yukon salmon fisheries have been restricted.

Scientists point to warming waters and changing ocean conditions, not trawl bycatch, as the primary causes of the declines. Warmer oceans can increase the risk of salmon bycatch by changing where salmon and pollock overlap, according to a study last year.

Critics say bycatch is one of the few sources of fish mortality managers can directly control, and even small losses matter when runs are depleted.

“Each fish is critical to communities along the Yukon River,” said Andrew Seitz, professor of fisheries at the University of Alaska Fairbanks. “The people who feel that they bear the brunt of the conservation measures are people along the river.”

AVOIDING SALMON

During the four days reporters spend aboard F/V Progress, the vessel caught 210 chum salmon. Blake, who has 13 years in the pollock industry, said avoiding salmon is a central part of his job. He said the search for waters with fewer salmon burned almost 3,000 gallons (11,360 liters) of fuel. Had he stayed put, he said, the boat could have filled its holds in half a day with far less.

“The subsistence users see this huge machine industry out here harvesting in the ocean and I can understand their frustration,” he said. “I would be upset if somebody told me that I wasn’t allowed to fish like my ancestors had done for thousands of years before.”

Blake and industry representatives call it one of the best managed fisheries in the world. Captains stay in contact with other vessels throughout each trip to share information about salmon concentrations, while the fleet follows weekly closure areas based on reports from the fishing grounds. Pollock vessels carry salmon excluders, devices which help salmon find a way out of the net.

Every salmon caught by the Bering Sea pollock fleet is counted. Trawlers are monitored by observers or cameras, as are deliveries at shoreside processing plants.

“The amount of science and management effort that goes into improving it is basically unprecedented anywhere,” said Matt Tinning, CEO of the At-Sea Processors Association, which represents five Alaska pollock companies. “The system is designed to really incentivize salmon avoidance every day, all the time.”

FLIP SIDE

At 9am on a July morning in Rampart, an Alaska Native village, about a dozen boats sat moored along the Yukon River. In years past, families would have been pulling nets and carrying salmon to their smokehouses.

The Yukon flows 2,010km across Alaska before emptying into the Bering Sea. Salmon born in its tributaries migrate to the ocean, spend years feeding at sea, then return to spawn, linking villages such as Rampart to the same waters where the pollock fleet fishes.

“We have this big void in our lives right now,” said Brooke Woods, a Koyukon Alaska Native, mother of six and commissioner for the Yukon River Inter-Tribal Fish Commission. “We’ve never had a generation that hasn’t had the opportunity to learn and be taught by elders and parents, and that has such a big impact on our youth.”

Woods’ family once spent long summer days checking nets, cutting fish and tending the smokehouse. This summer, her three-year-old son, Lewis, watched TV and played in the creek behind the house. He has never set a salmon net with his parents.

Restrictions on their own harvest are difficult to accept when pollock trawlers are fishing offshore.

“You really get angry. Why are we the only ones that have to take the burden?” said Brooke’s mother, Janet Woods.

Rampart has no grocery store, and reaching Fairbanks takes about five hours by boat and road. Families stock up when they travel and have long relied on fishing and hunting to fill their freezers.

Managers briefly opened chum fishing around Rampart this summer, but only with selective gear such as dip nets and beach seines. The Woods family did not have that equipment.

“You think back in history how they tried to destroy us,” Janet said. “Taking our language, our ceremonies, and now our culture, and it’s been forever a fight for us just to hang on to what very little we have.”

SOURCING FISH

Fish from across the North Pacific mix in the Bering Sea, so a salmon caught in a trawl net could have come from western Alaska, the Pacific Northwest or as far away as Russia or Japan.

NOAA has long used genetic testing to trace salmon bycatch. Since 2024, the Bristol Bay Science and Research Institute has produced weekly chum bycatch estimates from summer to fall to give the fleet faster information about where western Alaska salmon are showing up.

The results support one of the industry’s main arguments: Most chum caught by pollock trawlers are not from western Alaska. In the past few years, western Alaska fish made up an average of about 17 percent of chum and half of Chinook bycatch.

Even a small share means tens of thousands of salmon. In 2021, for example, 9 percent of chum bycatch came from western Alaska, or more than 51,000 salmon, according to NOAA.

In February, after hearing testimony from more than 170 people, the North Pacific Fishery Management Council, which sets many of the rules for the Bering Sea fleet, recommended a cap of 45,000 western Alaska chum bycatch. Critics said the limit was too high.

Pollock is big business in Alaska. More than 3 billion pounds (1.36 million tonnes) were landed from the Bering Sea and Gulf of Alaska in 2024, worth about US$432 million, according to NOAA. While the fishery supports thousands of Alaska jobs, critics said most of the economic benefit flows outside the state, with many of the largest vessels owned by Seattle-area companies.

“We’re trying to play this balancing game” between helping conserve western Alaska salmon for subsistence communities and maintaining “a very valuable economic fishery,” said Abby Duffy, who manages the Bristol Bay institute’s genetics lab in Dutch Harbor.

WIDESPREAD ISSUES

Small commercial halibut and crab fishers as well as charter operators have echoed the grievances heard along the Yukon. They too have faced shrinking catch limits and closures as stocks decline, while groundfish trawlers continue to catch both species as bycatch.

Last year alone, Alaska trawl fisheries discarded about 96 million pounds (43,500 tonnes) of bycatch, according to the North Pacific Fishery Management Council. That is about 100 fully loaded Boeing 747-8s.

“It’s extremely frustrating,” said Linda Behnken, a commercial fisher and executive director of the Alaska Longline Fishermen’s Association.

The larger concern is what trawling does to the seafloor, she said.

“The habitat damage is really insidious and long lasting,” she said.

Pollock vessels use pelagic, or midwater, trawls that are designed to fish in the water column rather than along the seafloor the way bottom trawls do. But pollock often swim close to the seafloor, so the nets make substantial bottom contact. That contact was evident during the trip aboard the F/V Progress, when Tanner crabs and basket stars — animals that live on the seafloor — came up with the net.

Meanwhile, some of the same areas that are closed to bottom trawling for the protection of coral, sponges, crab and other marine life are open to pelagic trawlers.

“So they’re dragging in the same areas, defeating the whole purpose of these habitat conservation areas,” said Ben Enticknap, fisheries campaign director at Oceana.

GROWING ANGER

Anti-trawl sentiment has attracted Democrats, Republicans, commercial and sport fishers, and Alaska Native communities — constituencies that do not often line up on the same side of resource debates.

At least half the original candidates in Alaska’s crowded governor’s race took positions critical of trawling or bycatch as contenders across the political spectrum called for tighter restrictions. The governor has significant influence over federal fisheries policy with the power to nominate five of the North Pacific council’s seven appointed voting seats. Several gubernatorial candidates campaigned specifically on using those appointments to shift the council away from trawl interests.

In the US Senate race, Democrat Mary Peltola has called for an end to large factory trawlers, while Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan has introduced legislation aimed at reducing bycatch and keeping trawl gear off the seafloor.

Back in the Bering Sea, Blake kept fishing for pollock. Along the Yukon, the Woods family’s boat remained tied to the bank.

Blake hopes his son can one day fish beside him on the trawler. Brooke Woods hopes her son can one day set a salmon net with her.

“It’s frightening for me to not know if I’ll be able to pass on the same knowledge that my mother, grandmother and parents had,” Woods said. “I’ve heard elders say that if we lose our salmon, that assimilation has worked.”

data.title: AI directions leading to increasing calls for wilderness rescues
data.description:
The route up the Widowmaker Arete, a 518m cliff in British Columbia, is deceptively described as “mostly easy slab climbing,” interspersed with “short steep sections that can include finger cracks, blocky face climbing.” It requires careful planning and the right equipment.

When 16-year-old Bryce Vincent Gowryluk found himself facing its sheer headwall last week, he had neither. He had asked the artificial intelligence (AI) chatbot Claude for directions.

Gowryluk had to be rescued after those directions proved wildly incorrect, in the latest incident to raise questions about the reliance on digital maps for wilderness navigation.

On a Saturday morning, Gowryluk took a gondola up to the top of Grouse Mountain and, while ascending, asked Claude to plan a route to nearby Crown Mountain and back. After navigating scree and more than 600m of elevation gain, the summit promises panoramic views of Greater Vancouver, the Fraser valley and the Capilano watershed.

The trek takes eight hours and hiking guides warn it is not for beginners.

As Gowryluk, an indoor climber, navigated down the Crown Pass and up through Crater Slabs and into a boulder-strewn valley, the directions from Claude took him away from the planned course.

He found himself at the final headwall of the Widowmaker Arete — a climb that requires ropes, cams and a clear plan for ascent. As he climbed, Gowryluk soon realized the terrain was far too steep and that he was stuck at the base of a cliff. He phoned his mother, then called emergency services for help.

Police notified North Shore Rescue, which launched a helicopter, but Gowryluk was too close to the rock face for the rotors, so two members of the rescue team were hoisted down to lift him up. He was flown to the rescue base near the Cleveland Dam.

In their debrief the rescue crew said Gowryluk was “far off” his intended route. While the incident could be the first time a hiker got lost because of AI, it is the latest in a string of mishaps in the mountainous region of south-western British Columbia, where hikers increasingly rely on imprecise directions.

In July, three people were rescued after they planned a route on the Howe Sound Crest Trail using Google Maps, which gave them wildly inaccurate time estimates, suggesting a route that often takes as long as 14 hours could be done in just more than five.

Search manager Paul Markey said that mountaineers should not rely on the directions of AI, and that proper preparation was key.

“In this particular case, the boy had a headlamp. He had good clothing. He had a good pair of boots, spare battery and spare food. He was pretty well equipped for hiking and scrambling. But he was certainly not prepared or equipped for rock climbing,” Markey said.

“Claude in this particular situation, has never been in the area that this 16-year-old boy found himself in. Claude can only go so far with regard to describing what the area may be like,” Markey said. “There’s definitely a trend towards using electronic applications as opposed to map and compass skills. But there is really no substitute for good map and compass training and education.”

He said that in some cases, apps give too much information.

“We have found that some of the apps have identified trails in areas where, really, our preference as a rescue team would be that those trails or routes are not actually identified,” he said, adding that people see routes they think are good trails only to get into trouble.

“The main thing is: do not blindly rely on AI as a route planning tool,” Markey said. “It can never substitute for good education, good training, a good experience, good decision making in the field.”

data.title: Meta bans ads from TikTok on its apps
data.description:
ESCALATING FEUD: ‘We don’t have to run ads from a competitor whose goal is to pull people off our apps,’ a Meta spokesperson said about the complete restriction

Meta Platforms Inc banned advertisements in the US from ByteDance Ltd (字節跳動), the former controlling owner of TikTok, intensifying the competition with the popular social video site.

On Thursday, Meta began implementing a complete restriction on ads and paid marketing messages placed on its platforms by ByteDance, the Chinese company that remains in charge of key parts of TikTok in the US.

The ban is to take effect in the US, Canada, Egypt, Indonesia, Japan, Thailand and Vietnam, according to Meta, and also extend to third-party advertisers running campaigns that link to TikTok and other ByteDance properties in those countries.

“We don’t have to run ads from a competitor whose goal is to pull people off our apps,” Meta spokesperson Chris Sgro said in an e-mailed statement. “Declining promotional services to a competitor is a normal business practice across industries. We will continue to compete on product quality and user experience.”

Meta and TikTok have competed neck-and-neck for years, even with a key imbalance in that rivalry: TikTok has been able to operate in Meta’s most important market, the US, while Meta has been unable to do so in TikTok’s most crucial market, China. However, that competition took a more heated turn in August after Meta agreed to a historic US$18 billion settlement with US states requiring it to implement new safety features for minors across its Instagram and Facebook apps.

Since then, Meta has been pressuring TikTok and Google’s YouTube to commit to making similar changes, suggesting it cannot solve industrywide child safety problems on its own.

TikTok has remained publicly silent on the matter, ratcheting up the tension between the companies as Meta grapples with what it sees as yet another competitive disadvantage.

Last month, TikTok enacted a number of measures to make it harder to shift from its app to other social platforms, including by eliminating dedicated Instagram links from its users’ profiles. It also rejected ads from Meta demanding that TikTok commit to comparable concessions on child safety.

Soon after the settlement with the state attorneys general, Meta ran ads in top newspapers upping its pressure campaign. Meta executives have also called out TikTok publicly for failing to show up at a recent Office of the Surgeon General event on the harms of excessive screen use, and for dropping out of a national security meeting with the House Select Committee on China to avoid broader scrutiny amid its child safety litigation.

Other consumer tech platforms have also introduced friction between its products and its competitors. The Information reported last month that OpenAI told advertising partners that it would not accept ads for image and audio-generation products that competed with its own.

data.title: GlobalFoundries rallies after US$2bn TSMC deal
data.description:
PACKAGING PUSH: The chipmaker said that it would begin ramping up silicon interposer production in New York in the first half of 2028 to support AI systems

GlobalFoundries Inc shares gained as much as 7 percent after the chip manufacturer announced a five-year, US$2 billion deal to provide US production capacity to Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co (TSMC, 台積電).

Under the agreement, announced on Thursday, GlobalFoundries is to help supply components known as silicon interposers. The US company is to rely on manufacturing at its facility in Malta, New York, and said it has the option to expand capacity “as customer demand grows.”

An interposer is a small layer of silicon that sits between a chip and its packaging. It is home to the wires that carry electronic signals and power needed to make that chip functional. The components are increasingly important as semiconductors become larger and companies combine multiple chips into the same package.

GlobalFoundries expects to expand capacity at its Malta facility and establish the first US-based source of silicon interposers supporting advanced packaging technologies, including embedded deep trench capacitor components, it said.

The company expects to begin ramping up volume production of the TSMC components in the first half of 2028.

The multi-year US$2 billion agreement will expand capacity for advanced packaging ecosystem and support growing demand for AI and high-performance computing technologies, GlobalFoundries said.

The deal provides TSMC with an additional US-based source of production at a time when the Taiwanese company is working to expand its US footprint. TSMC is the dominant chip foundry — a business that produces semiconductors for outside customers — and serves clients such as Nvidia Corp, Apple Inc and Advanced Micro Devices Inc.

Shares of GlobalFoundries rose as high as US$51.45, marking their biggest intraday gain in three weeks. The stock had been up 38 percent this year through Wednesday’s close.

GlobalFoundries’ foundry business is generally focused on less sophisticated chips, what it calls “essential semiconductors.” Greater interest in technology like silicon interposers for packaging is giving the company a role to play in more advanced AI components.

“Advanced packaging is becoming increasingly critical to delivering the performance, power efficiency and scale required for next-generation AI systems,” GlobalFoundries senior vice president Ed Kaste said in the statement.

data.title: Vance highlights Microsoft in crackdown on visa abuse
data.description:
US President Donald Trump’s administration accused Microsoft Corp, Adobe Inc and a half-dozen other companies of abusing a US worker visa program and suspended them indefinitely from a longstanding immigration initiative that has served as a crucial talent pipeline for Silicon Valley and Wall Street.

The suspensions, announced on Thursday by US Vice President J.D. Vance and Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling, also target information technology services giants Cognizant Technology Solutions Corp, Infosys Ltd, Tata, Wipro Ltd, HCL Technologies Ltd and Capgemini SE. Those firms, either based in India or with large operations there, are often called outsourcers for their role offering contract IT work to other businesses.

At a briefing in Washington, Sonderling said there were multiple federal investigations under way into the use of a system that allows US employers to sponsor foreign workers for permanent residency.

“We are cutting off the head of the snake — the companies that enabled this abuse for decades,” Sonderling told reporters at Thursday’s briefing.

Vance singled out Microsoft, the world’s third-most valuable company, for what he characterized as exploitation of the program.

“There has been no company in the United States, unfortunately, that has abused this system more than Microsoft,” he said.

In a statement, Microsoft defended its use of visa programs and said that it looked forward to providing the administration with additional information. Adobe and the Indian companies named by Vance and Sonderling did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Vance’s comments assailing Microsoft came hours before Trump honored the company’s chief executive officer, Satya Nadella, with a National Medal of Technology and Innovation at a summit in Washington intended to spotlight US scientific leadership. Just last week, Nadella joined other tech industry leaders at a White House luncheon to discuss safeguards for artificial intelligence.

“Microsoft is a great American company, and we have a great relationship with them, they do a lot of important things,” Vance said. “Our message to Microsoft is not that we want to harm your company. It’s that we want your company to thrive, but we want it to thrive by employing and empowering your fellow Americans.”

The moves announced by Vance and Sonderling take aim at the Permanent Labor Certification Program, or PERM, which allows companies to sponsor a foreigner who has been working in the US under the H-1B and other visa holders to become a legal permanent resident, the first step to becoming a US citizen.

Silicon Valley’s reliance on foreign workers has long been a flashpoint in the debate over immigration. Since Trump’s return to office last year, the administration has seized on those concerns and pressed tech giants to do more to train and hire US workers.

As part of that effort, Trump has moved to make it harder for companies to use H-1B visas to attract foreign talent, targeting a major source of workers for the industry. The changes have included proposals for $100,000 filing fees for most candidates and tightening the rules of how the H-1B visas are awarded in an annual lottery, giving priority to companies offering the highest salaries.

Vance urged the US-based companies to shift their policies to employ more US workers.

“Stop defrauding the American worker. Stop importing an indentured servant to do a job that an American worker would happily do,” the vice president said.

data.title: OpenAI expects US$70bn in annualized revenue
data.description:
OpenAI is expecting to reach or exceed US$70 billion in annualized revenue by the end of the year, according to people familiar with the matter, driven largely by growth in its enterprise business.

The ChatGPT maker’s annualized revenue was roughly US$50 billion at the end of last month, the people said. The figure represents a projection of OpenAI’s yearly sales based on a shorter period.

The company shared the numbers with investors as part of discussions for its latest fundraising effort, said the people, requesting anonymity to discuss private information.

The company is in talks to raise US$30 billion or more at a US$1.4 trillion valuation before the new money, Bloomberg first reported last month.

OpenAI declined to comment.

OpenAI, Anthropic and other AI firms have often touted their annualized revenue as a key growth metric. However, not all companies measure it the same way. Anthropic’s annualized revenue hit US$65 billion by the end of July, Bloomberg News previously reported.

Some outlets reported last month that OpenAI was already projecting nearly US$70 billion in annualized revenue, based on investor estimates.

The Financial Times reported on Thursday that the discrepancy came from OpenAI’s investors attempting to calculate OpenAI’s annualized revenue using the same methods as rival Anthropic PBC, which accounts for sales from cloud providers differently.

On Thursday, tech shares led losses in the S&P 500 after reports that OpenAI’s annualized revenue would be lower than some previous estimates. The NASDAQ 100 fell 1.4 percent. A gauge of chip giants sank 3.4 percent.

While OpenAI has pushed back plans for an initial public offering until at least next year, citing its focus on AI safety efforts, Anthropic is expected to sell shares in an IPO as soon as next month.

OpenAI is in talks with multiple investment funds from the United Arab Emirates, including Abu Dhabi-based MGX, to help anchor its new financing round, Bloomberg has reported.

The company most recently raised a US$122 billion round in March at an US$852 billion valuation, including the money.

data.title: AI valuation fears derail Firmus IPO
data.description:
Firmus Grid Ltd abandoned its attempt at one of Australia’s biggest-ever initial public offerings, after the Nvidia Corp-backed data center company failed to lure global investors who have grown increasingly skittish over frothy AI valuations.

It was a dramatic about-face for a company that just days ago was signaling healthy demand for a deal that would have valued it at US$30 billion, up from US$10.5 billion less than three months ago. The canceled deal is a stark example of investor pushback against AI financing terms that some worry have become too generous as global borrowing costs climb and the long-term payoff from the technology remains uncertain.

Firmus, whose business model hinges on a steady influx of fresh capital, will withdraw its application to list on the Australian Securities Exchange and consider other funding options, according to a statement yesterday.

“Having considered recent market volatility and prevailing market conditions, the board determined that the terms on which the offer could proceed would not appropriately reflect the strength of the company’s business and long-term growth outlook,” it said.

The IPO showed signs of stress soon after books opened for institutional investors this week. The struggles underscored investors’ polarized views on the deal. Some saw the business as well placed to benefit from the artificial intelligence boom, while others are worried about the valuation and existing shareholders potentially flooding the market soon after the debut. Part of the difficulty was convincing potential investors of the steep increase in market value for a company without a proven track record that had revenue of US$51 million in the 2026 financial year.

AI FACTORIES

Firmus, which was looking to raise as much as US$5.5 billion including a greenshoe option, must now find other ways to raise funds to keep its ambitious expansion plans on track. The company aims to build data centers it calls AI factories using hardware from backer Nvidia. It has a pipeline of 912 megawatts, of which only 46MW has been built, according to investor documents seen by Bloomberg.

“Investors just weren’t prepared to pay a sky-high price up front for capacity that’s still largely on the drawing board,” eToro lead analyst for APAC and Middle East Josh Gilbert said. “The timing hasn’t helped either, with higher yields lifting borrowing costs and shrinking what investors will pay today for earnings that sit years down the track.”

Firmus will also explore a potential listing in the US in the longer term, people familiar with the matter have said.

DATA CENTER PIPELINE

The failed deal underscores growing concern over how much capital AI infrastructure companies are demanding from public markets at a time when borrowing costs are rising. Much of Firmus’ valuation was based on the company successfully building a pipeline of data centers across Asia serving customers such as Meta Platforms Inc and OpenAI.

The strain is spreading across credit markets in the US, where a record wave of AI-related borrowing is forcing investors to reassess the risks around some of the biggest technology companies. Nearly US$500 billion of new debt has been priced this year to fund AI infrastructure, while rising financing needs and interest rates have driven up credit-insurance costs and weakened tech debt performance.

“There’s no question investors feel more anxiety recently, as the tech sector rallies despite mounting risk on every other front,” Rayliant Global Advisors head of portfolio management Phillip Wool wrote in a LinkedIn post. “Everything at this point hinges on the virtuous cycle of AI infrastructure spending boosting hardware and hyperscalers’ AI investment exciting shareholders about their own future earnings growth.”

data.title: Book nook
data.description: People visit a booth at the 78th Frankfurt Book Fair, the world’s biggest trade fair for books, in Frankfurt am Main, Germany, yesterday. The fair ends tomorrow. It allows publishing experts meet up with partners from the technology and creative industries such as film and games at one of the world’s leading venues for printed and digital content. The Czech Republic is this year’s guest of honor.

data.title: Exports hit record amid AI demand
data.description:
MONTHLY HIGH: Shipments have risen for 35 straight months, extending Taiwan’s longest uninterrupted growth streak, despite trade policies and geopolitical risks

Taiwan’s exports rose to a record last month as booming demand for artificial intelligence (AI) servers and other high-tech products powered shipments, putting the economy on track for another year of exceptionally strong trade growth.

Exports jumped 60.9 percent from a year earlier to US$87.22 billion last month, the highest monthly figure on record, the Ministry of Finance said yesterday.

Shipments have risen for 35 straight months, extending Taiwan’s longest uninterrupted growth streak.

The latest surge was led by AI-related products, with demand offsetting uncertainty over global trade policy and geopolitical tensions, Department of Statistics Director-General Beatrice Tsai (蔡美娜) said.

Exports of information, communications and audio-video products more than doubled from a year earlier, with shipments of graphics cards, servers, storage devices, switches and routers all posting triple-digit growth, the ministry said.

Electronic components were also a major source of momentum, rising 45.3 percent as AI applications and preparations for new consumer electronics products boosted demand, it said.

Third-quarter exports surged 44.6 percent year-on-year to US$244.92 billion, exceeding the government’s August forecast and suggesting room for an upward revision to its 11.05 percent GDP growth forecast for this year.

“The growth momentum is expected to continue in October,” Tsai said, adding that exports are expected to rise to 40 to 44 percent from a year earlier, potentially reaching another record.

Shipments of non-tech products also improved, although textile products bucked the trend, ministry data showed.

The US and Southeast Asia were the biggest contributors to last month’s export growth, with shipments to the US more than doubling, while exports to Southeast Asia jumped 93.4 percent from a year earlier.

The markets accounted for about 70 percent of the increase in total exports as global supply chains continued to realign, Tsai said.

Shipments to China, including Hong Kong, as well as Europe and Japan also posted double-digit gains.

Imports rose 51.7 percent to a record US$63.59 billion last month, leaving Taiwan with a monthly trade surplus of US$23.63 billion, also an all-time high, the data showed.

The outlook for exports remains strong for this quarter as cloud-service providers and governments accelerate investment in AI infrastructure, which is supporting demand for semiconductors, servers and related components, Tsai said.

The year-end shopping season in China, Europe and the US should provide an additional boost, she said.

Still, shifts in global trade policy and geopolitical tensions remain key risks to the outlook, Tsai added.

In the first nine months of this year, exports soared 46.2 percent from the same period last year to US$661.55 billion, topping the full-year figure of US$640.69 billion last year.

Imports rose 41.3 percent to about US$501 billion over the same period, the data showed.

data.title: TSMC quarterly revenue surges to NT$1.49 trillion
data.description:
SECOND-TOP MONTH: September revenue was 0.6 percent lower month-on-month, but despite the drop, it was the firm’s highest-ever sales report for the month

Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co (TSMC, 台積電) yesterday reported record quarterly revenue for last quarter, after sales last month hit the second-highest monthly level in the company’s history.

Revenue in the quarter ended last month was NT$1.49 trillion (US$46.75 billion), up 17 percent from NT$1.27 trillion in the second quarter and exceeding the combined prediction of 19 LSEG SmartEstimate analysts of NT$1.46 trillion.

Last quarter’s figure — which was up 12 percent from the midpoint of last year — also surpassed the company’s July estimates of US$44.6 billion to US$45.8 billion amid surging demand for the ramp-up of its advanced 2-nanometer technology, artificial intelligence (AI) chips and high-performance computing applications.

Last month, revenue was 0.6 percent lower month-on-month at NT$511.86 billion, the company said in a statement.

However, while the figure dropped from August, it was the highest-ever sales report for September in the company’s history.

In the first nine months of this year, cumulative revenue surged 41.1 percent to NT$3.9 trillion from NT$2.76 trillion in the same period last year, putting the company on track to hit its 40 percent annual growth target.

TSMC supplies chips to leading technology companies, including Nvidia Corp, Apple Inc and Advanced Micro Devices Inc.

The company is to disclose detailed financial figures for last quarter, as well as its business outlook for this quarter and next year during an earnings conference on Thursday next week.

At the earnings conference, the company’s overseas expansion plans and its comments on recent speculation surrounding new chip fabs in Texas would also be closely watched.

Yuanta Securities Investment Consulting Co (元大投顧) said that it expects TSMC’s third-quarter net profit to grow 66.5 percent year-on-year to NT$752.86 billion, compared with a 64 percent rise to NT$740.8 billion predicted by LSEG SmartEstimate.

TSMC is expected to hike capital expenditure to US$80 billion next year and US$100 billion in 2028, compared with US$60 billion to US$64 billion earmarked for this year, Yuanta said in a note on Wednesday.

This quarter, TSMC’s revenue is expected to grow 10 to 15 percent sequentially to about NT$1.66 trillion, fueled by Nvidia Corp’s new Rubin AI graphics processing units, AI custom chips and new 2-nanometer smartphone application processors, Yuanta said.

Driven by capacity constraints and strong AI-related demand, TSMC is expected to raise prices for advanced chips by 5 to 10 percent next year, and to increase prices for chips made on mature nodes by as much as 5 percent, Yuanta added.
